source_review.notes: Reviewed eight references covering integration patterns, web APIs, CSV, secure hashes, Parquet, data-intensive systems, data warehousing, and security log management. Official RFC Editor, NIST, Apache/GitHub, and Enterprise Integration Patterns endpoints returned HTTP 200. RFC 4180 is correctly identified as the October 2005 informational CSV document and the RFC Editor records its RFC 7111 update. NIST identifies FIPS 180-4 as the August 2015 final publication and notes a planned revision; the chapter cites the dated publication and makes no newest-edition claim.

evidence: Reviewed delivery, producer, schema, mode, scope, cutoff, predecessor, part-set, control-vector, object-version, byte, record, digest, range, rate, time, and reconciliation notation.
Confirmed decimal GB and MB units, record counts, seconds, processing windows, and lower-bound qualifications are stated.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Delivery identity, producer run, consumer run, part, source state, and visible target version remain distinct.

evidence: Recomputed 180000000 times 240 bytes as 43.2 GB and the 200 MB/s lower bound as 216 seconds.
Recomputed 800 times 256 MB as 204800 MB, two-hour necessary throughput as 28.44 MB/s, and twice-rate planning figure as 56.89 MB/s.
Recomputed Exercise 2 as 230400 MB, 42.67 MB/s necessary average, 3291.43 seconds or 54.86 minutes at 70 MB/s, and 35.14 minutes nominal margin.
numerical_recomputation.notes: Every arithmetic result is explicitly limited by compression, parsing, validation, staging, indexing, replication, contention, skew, retries, and late arrival.

evidence: Verified raw size as record count times average bytes, lower-bound scan or transfer time as bytes divided by sustained rate, and necessary window capacity as bytes divided by window.
Verified manifest completeness quantifies only declared immutable object versions and reconciliation-vector equality proves only its declared controls.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The chapter does not infer semantic equivalence or window success from byte arithmetic or control-vector equality.

evidence: Reviewed interruption during creation, upload, manifest publication, download, decompression, staging, validation, target commit, acknowledgment, and cleanup.

Reviewed missing, additional, duplicate, truncated, reordered, mutated, corrupt, late, overlapping, and gap-containing deliveries; schema, encoding, timezone, and key changes; and backfill contention.

Reviewed digest substitution, replay, path traversal, decompression bombs, formula injection, oversized fields, privacy leakage, key rotation, quarantine saturation, and safety-critical stale snapshots.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Examples cover structural, semantic, capacity, security, privacy, recovery, and high-consequence temporal failures.

evidence: Traced identity, completeness, publication, integrity, delta, restart, reconciliation, capacity, security, and evidence invariants through exposition, examples, and answers.
Confirmed checksum, signature, encryption, schema validation, row count, scheduler success, transfer success, and consumer acknowledgment retain distinct evidence limits.
invariant_checking.notes: Snapshot, delta, manifest, part, correction, quarantine, and published target semantics remain distinct.

evidence: Reviewed the completeness argument: without a terminal claim, a consumer cannot distinguish a slow producer from a completed smaller delivery by part visibility alone.
Confirmed immutable exact object versions plus a terminal manifest make completeness verifiable under the storage guarantees without claiming business correctness.
Reviewed restart and delta reasoning and confirmed stable identities and predecessor detection are necessary but still require transactional or isolated publication mechanisms.
proof_review.notes: No filesystem or object-store atomicity is assumed without platform verification, and no checksum or reconciliation total is elevated to universal correctness proof.

evidence: Audited uses of atomic, immutable, durable, complete, consistent, authentic, authoritative, safe, guarantee, proof, invariant, and evidence.
Verified lower bounds, necessary capacity, digest evidence, signatures, manifests, and control totals all retain explicit scope.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Models, storage mechanisms, policy, security evidence, and business outcomes are kept distinct.

empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: The chapter prescribes transfer, failure, recovery, security, compatibility, and reconciliation tests but presents no executed code, live storage system, benchmark, or reproduced empirical study.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed batch selection, logical delivery, snapshot and delta semantics, cutoffs, immutable publication, manifests, integrity and authenticity, layered validation, staging, reconciliation, rejects, restart, capacity, part size, evolution, security, observation, failure testing, acknowledgment, retention, and hybrid integration for conceptual coherence.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed partial uploads, listing races, manifest canonicalization, digest substitution, decompression limits, direct-live-load hazards, duplicate resubmission, delta gaps, mixed time zones, quarantine exposure, disk and quota exhaustion, overlapping runs, backfill starvation, key rotation, rollback, restore, and partner reconciliation. Internal practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified first-principles batch vocabulary, explicit delivery and capacity models, sixteen misconceptions, ten distinct worked examples, and five progressive exercises with complete answers ending in an unfamiliar cross-border disaster-relief transfer problem.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external academic or practitioner review is claimed. Source reachability, arithmetic, and structural review do not constitute an end-to-end storage or transfer experiment.
